directAnswer: Pope John III was a Roman cleric, born Catelinus, who led the Church from 561 to 574. His pontificate coincided with the Lombard invasion of Italy in 568, and the little that survives about him comes chiefly from the Liber Pontificalis and from Gregory of Tours.

sections.h2: Catelinus and the Lombard Invasion of 568
paras: John III was a Roman by birth, the son of a man named Anastasius, and he bore the personal name Catelinus before taking the name John on his election. He followed Pope Pelagius I and, like his predecessors in the years after Justinian's reconquest, governed the Roman Church as a subject of the Eastern Roman Empire.

Only a few years into his reign the Lombards under King Alboin crossed into northern Italy in 568, beginning a conquest that would reshape the peninsula for two centuries. Imperial defenses were thin, and Rome itself was exposed. The Liber Pontificalis reports that John traveled to Naples to persuade the general Narses, who had fallen out with the Roman population, to return to Rome, apparently judging that the city needed his protection more than it needed the quarrel.

sections.h2: Retreat to the Via Appia and an Appeal from Gaul
paras: The same source says that after this episode John withdrew for a time to the church of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian on the Via Appia, outside the city, and carried out ordinations there. Historians are unsure of the exact reasons, though tensions in Rome after Narses' return seem the likeliest explanation. He is also credited with care for the catacombs and with seeing to it that Mass continued to be offered at the martyrs' shrines.

Gregory of Tours records one case that shows the reach of Roman appeals in this period: two Gallic bishops, Salonius of Embrun and Sagittarius of Gap, deposed by a synod at Lyon, appealed to John, who ordered them restored. John also completed the church of the Holy Apostles in Rome, begun under Pelagius I. He died in July 574 and was buried in St. Peter's. Beyond these points, little reliable detail about his thirteen-year pontificate has come down to us.

keyFacts: Reign: 17 July 561 – 13 July 574
Born in Rome; personal name Catelinus
Pontificate saw the Lombard invasion of Italy (568)
Completed the church of the Holy Apostles (Santi Apostoli) in Rome
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: Why did Pope John III change his name?
faqs.answer: He was born Catelinus and took the name John when he became pope. He is often listed as the second pope known to have taken a new name, after John II, who was born Mercurius.

faqs.question: What happened in Italy during John III's reign?
faqs.answer: The Lombards invaded northern Italy in 568 and steadily took territory from the Eastern Roman Empire. Rome was left vulnerable, and John's dealings with the general Narses reflect the city's search for protection.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict I was a Roman who served as pope from 575 to 579, during the Lombard advance through Italy. His reign is remembered mainly for famine in Rome and for his reliance on the emperor in Constantinople for relief, as recorded in the Liber Pontificalis.

sections.h2: A Long Wait for Imperial Confirmation
paras: Benedict was a Roman, the son of a man named Boniface according to the Liber Pontificalis. After the death of John III in July 574, nearly eleven months passed before his consecration in June 575. In this period a newly elected pope needed the emperor's approval before he could be consecrated, and with the Lombards cutting the roads of central Italy, messages to and from Constantinople moved slowly.

sections.h2: Famine and Lombard Pressure on Rome
paras: The four years of his pontificate were hard ones for the city. The Lombards controlled much of the countryside, and Rome suffered from famine. The Liber Pontificalis records that Emperor Justin II sent grain ships from Egypt to relieve the hunger, an indication that the pope and the Roman population still looked to the imperial government as their chief source of help.

The same source notes that Benedict ordained a number of priests, deacons, and bishops, and that he died in the summer of 579 while the Lombards were pressing on Rome. He was buried in St. Peter's. No writings of his survive, and historians know almost nothing else about his personal life or his decisions as pope; his pontificate is an example of how sparse the record becomes in the late sixth century.

keyFacts: Reign: 2 June 575 – 30 July 579
Born in Rome
Consecration delayed by the need for imperial confirmation
Rome suffered famine; Emperor Justin II sent grain from Egypt
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: Why was Benedict I's consecration delayed?
faqs.answer: Popes of this era needed the Eastern emperor's confirmation before consecration. The Lombard invasion made communication with Constantinople slow, so almost a year passed between John III's death and Benedict's consecration.

faqs.question: How did Rome survive famine under Benedict I?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, Emperor Justin II sent grain from Egypt to feed the city while the Lombards controlled much of the surrounding countryside.

directAnswer: Pope Pelagius II, a Roman of Gothic descent, reigned from 579 to 590 while the Lombards threatened Rome. He sought help from Constantinople through his envoy, the future Pope Gregory the Great, rebuilt the basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura, and died in the plague of 590.

sections.h2: Consecrated Under Lombard Siege
paras: Pelagius was born in Rome, the son of a man the Liber Pontificalis calls Unigild, a Gothic name that points to a family of Ostrogothic origin settled in the city. He was elected while the Lombards were besieging Rome and was consecrated without waiting for the emperor's confirmation, since the siege made it impossible to obtain in time. Once the siege lifted, he sent a delegation to Constantinople to explain the circumstances.

Protecting Rome became the central task of his pontificate. Pelagius sent the deacon Gregory, later Pope Gregory I, to the imperial court as his permanent representative (apocrisiarius) to plead for troops and funds. When little help came, he urged the bishop of Auxerre and others in Gaul to press the Franks to act against the Lombards.

sections.h2: The Three Chapters Schism and the Title of Ecumenical Patriarch
paras: In northern Italy, bishops of the province of Aquileia had broken communion with Rome over the condemnation of the Three Chapters at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Pelagius wrote to them at length, with letters thought to have been drafted with Gregory's help, arguing that the council had not undermined the Council of Chalcedon. The effort did not end the schism, which lasted for many decades more.

He also objected when Patriarch John IV of Constantinople used the title Ecumenical Patriarch at a synod in 588, and he refused to accept the synod's acts on that point. Gregory would continue the same protest as pope. During Pelagius' reign the Visigothic king Reccared embraced Catholic Christianity, and the Third Council of Toledo in 589 brought the Visigothic kingdom of Spain into the Catholic fold.

sections.h2: San Lorenzo fuori le Mura and the Plague of 590
paras: Pelagius rebuilt the basilica over the tomb of St. Lawrence on the road to Tivoli. The triumphal arch mosaic of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura still shows him holding a model of the church and presenting it to Christ, one of the few surviving images of a sixth-century pope. He also turned his own house into a hospice for the poor and the elderly, according to the Liber Pontificalis.

In late 589 the Tiber flooded, and a plague followed in Rome. Pelagius died of it on 7 February 590 and was buried in St. Peter's. The Roman clergy and people then chose Gregory, his former envoy, as his successor.

keyFacts: Reign: 26 November 579 – 7 February 590
Born in Rome to a family of Gothic origin
Sent the future Gregory the Great as envoy to Constantinople
Rebuilt the basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura, where his mosaic portrait survives
Died in the Roman plague of 590

faqs.question: How was Pelagius II connected to Gregory the Great?
faqs.answer: Pelagius made Gregory a deacon and sent him to Constantinople as his envoy. Gregory helped draft some of his letters and was elected to succeed him after Pelagius died in the plague of 590.

faqs.question: Is there a picture of Pope Pelagius II?
faqs.answer: Yes. The mosaic on the triumphal arch of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura in Rome depicts him offering a model of the rebuilt basilica to Christ.

faqs.question: Why did Pelagius II object to the title Ecumenical Patriarch?
faqs.answer: When the patriarch of Constantinople used the title at a synod in 588, Pelagius saw it as a claim to authority over the whole Church and rejected the synod's acts on that point.

directAnswer: Pope St. Gregory I, called Gregory the Great, led the Church from 590 to 604. A former prefect of Rome turned monk, he defended the city during the Lombard wars, sent St. Augustine of Canterbury to evangelize the English, and wrote the Pastoral Rule, the Dialogues, and the Moralia on Job. He is a Doctor of the Church and one of the four great Latin Fathers.

sections.h2: From Prefect of Rome to the Monastery of St. Andrew
paras: Gregory was born in Rome around 540 to a wealthy patrician family. His father, Gordianus, held office in the Roman Church, and his mother, Silvia, is venerated as a saint. Sources trace his ancestry to Pope Felix III. He received a strong education in law and letters and, by about 573, was serving as prefect of the city, the highest civil post in Rome.

Soon afterward he gave up public life. He turned the family home on the Caelian Hill into a monastery dedicated to St. Andrew, founded several more on family estates in Sicily, and lived as a monk. Pope Pelagius II drew him back into Church service, ordaining him a deacon and sending him to Constantinople as papal envoy for several years. He returned to St. Andrew's in the mid-580s, and in 590, after Pelagius died in a plague, the clergy and people elected him pope despite his reluctance.

sections.h2: Servant of the Servants of God in a City at War
paras: Gregory took office in a ruined and frightened city. With imperial officials in Ravenna slow to act, he organized the defense of Rome, negotiated with the Lombard dukes and King Agilulf, and paid for peace when necessary. He managed the Church's large estates across Italy and Sicily so that their income fed the poor, ransomed captives, and supplied grain to Rome. His more than 850 surviving letters show a pope deeply involved in practical administration.

He described himself as servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God, a phrase that became a standard papal title. In the same spirit he protested, as Pelagius II had done, when Patriarch John the Faster of Constantinople used the title Ecumenical Patriarch, seeing it as a claim no single bishop should make.

sections.h2: The Mission to the English
paras: In 596 Gregory sent Augustine, prior of his own monastery of St. Andrew, with a group of monks to the Anglo-Saxons. They landed in Kent in 597, where King Æthelberht, whose wife Bertha was already a Christian, received them and was baptized. Gregory sent further missionaries and practical guidance, including the advice, preserved by Bede, that pagan temples be purified and reused as churches rather than destroyed. Augustine became the first archbishop of Canterbury, and the English long honored Gregory as their apostle.

sections.h2: The Pastoral Rule, the Dialogues, and the Moralia
paras: Gregory's writings shaped Christian thought for a thousand years. The Pastoral Rule (Regula Pastoralis) explains how a bishop should live and how he should adapt his preaching to different kinds of people; it was later translated into Old English under King Alfred. The Moralia, a vast commentary on the Book of Job, became a standard handbook of moral theology. His Homilies on the Gospels and on Ezekiel were widely read.

The Dialogues collect accounts of Italian holy men; Book II is the earliest life of St. Benedict of Nursia and the main source for what is known of him. The Dialogues are also the origin of the custom of the Gregorian Masses, thirty Masses offered on consecutive days for a deceased person. Tradition credits Gregory with organizing the Church's chant, which bears his name; historians agree he worked on the Roman liturgy, though Gregorian chant as we know it took its form in later centuries.

sections.h2: Doctor of the Church and Saint of East and West
paras: Gregory died on 12 March 604 and was buried in St. Peter's. He was acclaimed a saint immediately after his death. In 1298 Pope Boniface VIII named him, with Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church. Since the 1969 calendar reform his feast is kept on September 3, the anniversary of his episcopal consecration; it was formerly March 12, the date still observed in the East, where he is known as Gregory the Dialogist.

keyFacts: Reign: 3 September 590 – 12 March 604
Former prefect of Rome; founded the monastery of St. Andrew on the Caelian Hill
Sent St. Augustine to Kent in 596–597, beginning the conversion of the English
Wrote the Pastoral Rule, the Dialogues, the Moralia on Job, and over 850 surviving letters
Doctor of the Church (declared by Boniface VIII in 1298); feast day September 3

faqs.question: Why is Pope Gregory I called the Great?
faqs.answer: He earned the title for his defense and relief of Rome during the Lombard wars, his mission to England, his reform of Church administration, and writings that remained foundational for centuries. Only two other popes, Leo I and Nicholas I, are commonly called the Great.

faqs.question: Did St. Gregory the Great invent Gregorian chant?
faqs.answer: Tradition attributes the chant to him, and he did take an interest in the Roman liturgy. Most historians, however, think Gregorian chant developed its familiar form in the following centuries, especially in the Frankish kingdom.

faqs.question: What are Gregorian Masses?
faqs.answer: They are thirty Masses offered on thirty consecutive days for one deceased person. The practice traces back to a story Gregory tells in his Dialogues about a monk of his monastery who was freed from purgatory after such a series of Masses.

directAnswer: Pope Sabinian, born at Blera near Viterbo, succeeded Gregory the Great and reigned from 604 to 606. A former papal envoy to Constantinople, he became unpopular in Rome during a famine because he sold grain from Church stores rather than giving it away.

sections.h2: Gregory the Great's Envoy to Constantinople
paras: Sabinian came from Blera, a town in Tuscia north of Rome. Gregory the Great used him as a deacon and sent him as apocrisiarius, or papal representative, to the imperial court in Constantinople, though Gregory's letters suggest he was not always satisfied with his performance. Sabinian was elected soon after Gregory's death in March 604 but was not consecrated until September, after the emperor's approval arrived.

sections.h2: Grain, Famine, and an Unpopular Pontificate
paras: The Liber Pontificalis states that during a famine Sabinian opened the Church's granaries but sold the grain instead of distributing it freely, as Gregory had done. This made him deeply unpopular. The same source credits him with filling the churches with clergy, and he is generally thought to have favored the secular clergy over the monks Gregory had promoted.

Medieval writers added hostile legends, including a story that Gregory appeared to him in a vision to rebuke him; these tales are later inventions and say more about Sabinian's reputation than about events. It is reported that, when he died in February 606, his funeral procession had to leave the city walls to avoid a hostile crowd on its way to St. Peter's. Little else is reliably known of his brief reign.

keyFacts: Reign: 13 September 604 – 22 February 606
Born at Blera, near Viterbo
Served Gregory the Great as envoy to Constantinople
Criticized for selling Church grain during a famine
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: Why was Pope Sabinian unpopular?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, during a famine he sold grain from the Church's stores rather than distributing it free of charge, a sharp contrast with the generosity Romans remembered from Gregory the Great.

faqs.question: Is the story of Gregory the Great's ghost rebuking Sabinian true?
faqs.answer: No reliable early source supports it. The tale appears in later medieval writings and is best treated as legend reflecting Sabinian's poor reputation.

directAnswer: Pope Boniface III, a Roman of Greek descent, reigned for less than nine months in 607. A former envoy to Constantinople, he obtained from Emperor Phocas a recognition that the see of Rome was head of all the churches, and he held a synod regulating papal elections.

sections.h2: Envoy to the Court of Phocas
paras: Boniface was born in Rome to a family of Greek origin; the Liber Pontificalis names his father as John Cataadioce. Gregory the Great sent him to Constantinople as apocrisiarius, and there he gained the favor of Emperor Phocas. After Sabinian's death in February 606, almost a year passed before Boniface's consecration in February 607, a delay usually linked to waiting for imperial confirmation.

sections.h2: Rome as Head of All the Churches
paras: The Liber Pontificalis records that Boniface obtained a decree from Phocas declaring that the apostolic see of Peter was the head of all churches, in response to the patriarch of Constantinople's use of the title of ecumenical or universal bishop. The decree itself does not survive, and historians disagree about its exact wording and significance, but it reflects the long dispute begun under Pelagius II and Gregory I.

Boniface also held a synod in Rome attended by many bishops and clergy. It forbade anyone, under pain of excommunication, to discuss or arrange the election of a successor while a pope was still living, and it required that three days pass after a pope's burial before an election could take place. He died on 12 November 607 and was buried in St. Peter's. Little else about him is known.

keyFacts: Reign: 19 February 607 – 12 November 607
Born in Rome to a family of Greek descent
Former papal envoy to Emperor Phocas
Obtained an imperial decree recognizing Rome as head of all churches
Synod banned electioneering for a successor during a pope's lifetime

faqs.question: What did Boniface III obtain from Emperor Phocas?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, a decree stating that the see of Peter was head of all the churches. It answered the claims attached to the title of ecumenical patriarch used in Constantinople. The text of the decree has not survived.

faqs.question: What rules did Boniface III set for papal elections?
faqs.answer: His Roman synod prohibited discussing a pope's successor during his lifetime and ordered a waiting period of three days after a pope's burial before electing the next one.

directAnswer: Pope St. Boniface IV reigned from 608 to 615. Born in the region of the Marsi in central Italy, he is best known for converting the Pantheon in Rome into a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary and the martyrs, and for his contacts with the young English church and with St. Columbanus.

sections.h2: A Physician's Son from the Marsi
paras: Boniface came from the territory of the Marsi, in what is now Abruzzo; the Liber Pontificalis calls his father John a physician. He served as a deacon of the Roman Church under Gregory the Great, apparently with responsibility for its finances. After Boniface III's death, about ten months passed before his consecration in August 608. Some later sources describe him as a monk and say he turned his house into a monastery, which is why he is sometimes counted as a Benedictine, though this is not certain.

sections.h2: The Pantheon Becomes Santa Maria ad Martyres
paras: With the permission of Emperor Phocas, Boniface converted the ancient Pantheon, the temple of all the Roman gods, into a church dedicated to St. Mary and all the martyrs. Tradition places the dedication on 13 May 609 and holds that relics of martyrs were brought from the catacombs to the new church. The building survived intact largely because of this conversion, and the annual commemoration of the dedication is often cited as one root of the later feast of All Saints.

sections.h2: Mellitus, Columbanus, and a Troubled City
paras: In 610 Boniface held a synod in Rome on the life of monks and on the church in England, attended by Mellitus, bishop of London, who carried its decrees back to Britain. The Irish abbot Columbanus wrote him a famous, outspoken letter urging him to settle the controversy over the Three Chapters; it is one of the best-known documents of the early Irish church.

His reign saw famine, plague, and flooding in Rome. Boniface died on 8 May 615 and was buried in St. Peter's; his feast is kept on May 8. He was the first pope to take the same name as his immediate predecessor.

keyFacts: Reign: 25 August 608 – 8 May 615
Born in the region of the Marsi (Abruzzo)
Dedicated the Pantheon as the church of St. Mary and the Martyrs (traditionally 609)
Held a Roman synod in 610 attended by Mellitus of London
Feast day May 8

faqs.question: How is Pope Boniface IV connected to the Pantheon?
faqs.answer: He obtained the building from Emperor Phocas and dedicated it as a Christian church in honor of the Virgin Mary and the martyrs. It is still a church today, known as Santa Maria ad Martyres.

faqs.question: Did Boniface IV start All Saints Day?
faqs.answer: Not directly. The yearly commemoration of the Pantheon's dedication to Mary and the martyrs is often seen as one early influence, but the November 1 feast of All Saints developed later, especially in the eighth and ninth centuries.

faqs.question: Who was St. Columbanus to Boniface IV?
faqs.answer: Columbanus, an Irish abbot working on the Continent, wrote a frank letter to Boniface IV asking him to resolve the dispute over the Three Chapters and defend the faith vigorously.

directAnswer: Pope St. Adeodatus I, also called Deusdedit, was a Roman priest who reigned from 615 to 618. He favored the secular clergy of Rome, cared for the sick during an earthquake and epidemic, and is the earliest pope from whom a lead papal seal survives.

sections.h2: Forty Years a Priest of Rome
paras: Adeodatus, whose name is also given as Deusdedit (both mean given by God), was the son of a subdeacon named Stephen. The Liber Pontificalis says he had been a priest for about forty years before his election. Unlike Gregory the Great and Boniface IV, who had drawn heavily on monks, he restored the secular clergy to the positions they had held, a change many historians read as part of a lasting tension between the two groups in Rome.

sections.h2: Earthquake, Epidemic, and the First Papal Bullae
paras: In August 618 an earthquake struck Rome, and it was followed by an outbreak of a disease the sources describe as a kind of leprosy or scabies. The pope is remembered for personally caring for the afflicted. In his will, according to the Liber Pontificalis, he left a full year's stipend to his clergy, to be distributed at his funeral.

He is also the earliest pope from whom a lead seal survives. Such seals, called bullae, were attached to papal documents, and in time the documents themselves came to be called bulls. Adeodatus died on 8 November 618, his feast day, and was buried in St. Peter's. Little more is known.

keyFacts: Reign: 19 October 615 – 8 November 618
Born in Rome; also known as Deusdedit
Restored secular clergy to prominence in the Roman Church
Earliest surviving lead papal seal (bulla) is his
Feast day November 8

faqs.question: Is Pope Adeodatus I the same as Pope Deusdedit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adeodatus and Deusdedit are two forms of the same Latin name, both meaning given by God, and both are used for this pope. That is why the later Adeodatus II is sometimes called simply Adeodatus.

faqs.question: Why are papal documents called bulls?
faqs.answer: The name comes from the bulla, the lead seal attached to them. The oldest surviving papal lead seal belongs to Adeodatus I.

directAnswer: Pope Boniface V, a native of Naples, reigned from 619 to 625. He issued decrees on church asylum and the handling of relics, and, as Bede records, he supported the mission to the English, writing to King Edwin of Northumbria and granting the pallium to Archbishop Justus of Canterbury.

sections.h2: A Neapolitan Pope and His Decrees
paras: Boniface was born in Naples, the son of a man named John. After the death of Adeodatus I, more than a year passed before his consecration in December 619, during a period of unrest in Italy that included a revolt by the exarch Eleutherius. The Liber Pontificalis credits Boniface with decrees confirming the right of asylum in churches and ruling that acolytes were not to take the place of deacons in transferring the relics of martyrs. It also describes him as a gentle man who loved the clergy.

sections.h2: Letters to Northumbria and Canterbury
paras: Boniface's best-documented work concerns England, through letters that Bede copied into his Ecclesiastical History. He sent the pallium to Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, with authority to consecrate bishops. He also wrote to King Edwin of Northumbria, urging him to accept Christianity, and to Edwin's Christian queen Æthelburh of Kent, encouraging her to work for her husband's conversion. Edwin was baptized in 627, after Boniface's death.
Boniface died on 25 October 625 and was buried in St. Peter's. Apart from these records, little is known about him.

keyFacts: Reign: 23 December 619 – 25 October 625
Born in Naples
Issued decrees on church asylum and the translation of relics
Granted the pallium to Justus of Canterbury
Wrote to King Edwin of Northumbria and Queen Æthelburh, as recorded by Bede

faqs.question: What was Boniface V's role in the conversion of England?
faqs.answer: He supported the Canterbury mission by granting the pallium to Archbishop Justus and wrote to King Edwin of Northumbria and his queen urging the king's conversion. Edwin was baptized in 627, two years after Boniface died.

faqs.question: What is the right of asylum that Boniface V confirmed?
faqs.answer: It was the custom that a person fleeing danger or punishment could take refuge in a church and could not be removed by force. The Liber Pontificalis says Boniface V issued a decree upholding it.

directAnswer: Pope Honorius I, from Campania, reigned from 625 to 638. He was an energetic builder and a strong supporter of the English mission, but his letters to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople about the wills of Christ led the Third Council of Constantinople in 681 to condemn him posthumously for failing to oppose the Monothelite heresy.

sections.h2: A Builder and Patron of the English Church
paras: Honorius came from a noble family of Campania; his father, Petronius, held the rank of consul. As pope he followed the example of Gregory the Great in several ways, turning his family home into a monastery and taking an active part in the government of Rome. He enjoyed good relations with Emperor Heraclius, who allowed him to take gilded bronze tiles from the Temple of Venus and Roma to cover the roof of St. Peter's.

He rebuilt the basilica of Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura, whose apse mosaic still shows him holding a model of the church beside St. Agnes, and he restored or founded several other churches, including San Pancrazio on the Janiculum. In England, he sent the missionary Birinus, who converted the West Saxons, and in 634 he sent the pallium to Honorius of Canterbury and Paulinus of York. He also wrote to the Irish urging them to adopt the Roman date of Easter.

sections.h2: The Letters to Sergius on the One Will
paras: In the 630s Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople, seeking to reconcile Christians who rejected the Council of Chalcedon, promoted the idea that Christ had one activity and later one will. Sergius wrote to Honorius asking for support. In his reply, Honorius advised against speaking of one or two energies and used the phrase one will of Christ, apparently meaning that Christ's human will was never in conflict with the divine will.

Shortly before Honorius died in October 638, Emperor Heraclius issued the Ekthesis, a decree imposing belief in a single will. Honorius' successors condemned the Ekthesis and the teaching behind it, known as Monothelitism. Pope John IV defended Honorius' intentions, arguing that he had been misunderstood.

sections.h2: Condemnation at the Third Council of Constantinople
paras: In 681 the Third Council of Constantinople, the sixth ecumenical council, defined that Christ has two wills, human and divine, and anathematized the leading Monothelites, including Honorius. Pope Leo II confirmed the council but described Honorius' fault as negligence: he had failed to suppress the heresy as an apostolic bishop should, rather than having taught it himself. His name appeared in condemnations repeated by later councils and popes.

The case of Honorius was debated heavily before the First Vatican Council in 1870, as critics raised it against papal infallibility. Defenders responded that his letters were private pastoral advice, not a solemn definition binding the whole Church, and that his words could bear an orthodox meaning. Historians continue to discuss how much Honorius understood the issue at stake.

keyFacts: Reign: 27 October 625 – 12 October 638
Born in Campania to a consular family
Rebuilt Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura, where his mosaic portrait survives
Sent Birinus to Wessex; granted the pallium to Canterbury and York in 634
Anathematized posthumously by the Third Council of Constantinople (681)

faqs.question: Was Pope Honorius I a heretic?
faqs.answer: The Third Council of Constantinople anathematized him, but Pope Leo II, in confirming the council, explained his fault as failing to stamp out heresy rather than teaching it. Catholic theologians generally hold that his letters were not formal definitions of doctrine and can be read in an orthodox sense.

faqs.question: Does the case of Honorius disprove papal infallibility?
faqs.answer: This was argued at the time of the First Vatican Council. The council's defenders noted that infallibility applies only to solemn definitions on faith and morals addressed to the whole Church, and that Honorius' private letters to Sergius did not meet those conditions.

faqs.question: What churches did Honorius I build?
faqs.answer: He rebuilt Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura on the Via Nomentana and worked on several other Roman churches, including San Pancrazio. He also covered the roof of Old St. Peter's with bronze tiles taken from an ancient temple.

directAnswer: Pope Severinus was a Roman elected after the death of Honorius I in 638, but imperial resistance kept him from being consecrated until May 640, and he died that August. His short pontificate was overshadowed by pressure from Constantinople to accept the Monothelite Ekthesis and by the plundering of the Lateran treasury.

sections.h2: Held Hostage by the Ekthesis
paras: Severinus was a Roman, the son of a man named Avienus. He was chosen soon after Honorius I died in October 638, just as Emperor Heraclius issued the Ekthesis, a statement requiring belief in one will in Christ. Imperial officials withheld confirmation of the election, apparently hoping to obtain the new pope's acceptance of the decree. Envoys sent by the Roman clergy to Constantinople eventually secured approval by promising to bring the document to his attention, without committing him to sign it.

sections.h2: The Sack of the Lateran Treasury
paras: While the confirmation was delayed, the Liber Pontificalis reports, the imperial chartularius Maurice, with the support of the exarch Isaac of Ravenna, stirred up unpaid soldiers in Rome and seized the treasures of the Lateran palace, part of which was sent to the emperor. The episode shows how vulnerable the papacy was to imperial officials in Italy during this period.

Severinus was finally consecrated in May 640 and lived only about two months longer. The Liber Pontificalis describes him as holy, kind, and generous to the poor, and credits him with restoring the apse mosaic of St. Peter's. Some later sources say he rejected the Ekthesis, but this is not firmly documented. He died on 2 August 640 and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Reign: 15 October 638 – 2 August 640 (consecrated only in May 640)
Born in Rome, son of Avienus
Imperial confirmation delayed over the Monothelite Ekthesis
Lateran treasury plundered by imperial officials during the delay
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: Why did Pope Severinus wait so long to be consecrated?
faqs.answer: The imperial government delayed confirming his election, evidently to pressure him into accepting the Ekthesis, Emperor Heraclius' decree teaching one will in Christ. He was consecrated only in May 640, about a year and a half after his election.

faqs.question: Who plundered the Lateran under Severinus?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, the imperial official Maurice, backed by the exarch Isaac, used discontented soldiers to seize the Lateran treasury before Severinus was consecrated.

directAnswer: Pope John IV, a Dalmatian from Zadar, reigned from 640 to 642. He condemned Monothelitism at a Roman synod, defended the memory of his predecessor Honorius I, and spent Church funds to ransom captives taken in Slavic raids on Dalmatia and Istria.

sections.h2: A Dalmatian Archdeacon Opposes the One-Will Doctrine
paras: John was born in Dalmatia, traditionally at Zadar, the son of a scholasticus, or advocate, named Venantius. He was archdeacon of the Roman Church when elected and, while still pope-elect, joined other Roman clergy in a letter to the Irish church about the date of Easter and the Pelagian heresy, which Bede preserved in part.

Soon after his consecration in December 640, John held a synod in Rome that condemned Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will. He also wrote to Emperor Constantine III, Heraclius' son, defending Honorius I: in his view Honorius had meant only that Christ did not have the conflicting wills of fallen human nature, not that he lacked a human will.

sections.h2: Ransoming Captives and the Chapel of San Venanzio
paras: Slavic and Avar raids had devastated John's homeland. He sent an abbot named Martin with large sums to Dalmatia and Istria to ransom captives, and Martin brought back relics of martyrs from the ruined city of Salona. John built the oratory of San Venanzio beside the Lateran Baptistery to house them; its seventh-century apse mosaic, showing Dalmatian saints, survives and was completed under his successor Theodore I.
John died on 12 October 642 and was buried in St. Peter's. Little else is recorded of his personal life.

keyFacts: Reign: 24 December 640 – 12 October 642
Born in Dalmatia, traditionally at Zadar
Roman synod condemned Monothelitism
Wrote to Emperor Constantine III defending Honorius I
Built the Oratory of San Venanzio at the Lateran Baptistery for Dalmatian relics

faqs.question: Why did John IV defend Honorius I?
faqs.answer: Monothelites cited Honorius' letter to Sergius as support. John IV argued to the emperor that Honorius had been misunderstood and had not denied that Christ possessed a human will.

faqs.question: What is the Chapel of San Venanzio?
faqs.answer: It is an oratory next to the Lateran Baptistery in Rome, built by John IV to house relics of Dalmatian martyrs. Its apse mosaic from the seventh century can still be seen.

directAnswer: Pope Theodore I, a Greek born in Jerusalem, reigned from 642 to 649. A firm opponent of Monothelitism, he refused to recognize the patriarch of Constantinople, excommunicated the Monothelite patriarchs Pyrrhus and Paul II, and prepared the Lateran Council of 649, though he died before it met.

sections.h2: A Son of the Church of Jerusalem
paras: Theodore was born in Jerusalem, the son of a bishop also named Theodore, and was probably among the many Greek-speaking clergy who came to Rome after the Persian and Arab conquests of the eastern provinces. His election in 642 brought to Rome a pope with direct experience of the Christological disputes that divided the East. He was consecrated in November 642, apparently without a long wait for imperial approval.

sections.h2: Confronting Pyrrhus and Paul of Constantinople
paras: Theodore at once challenged the leadership in Constantinople. He refused to recognize Paul II as patriarch, arguing that his predecessor Pyrrhus had not been canonically deposed, and he urged the emperor to withdraw the Ekthesis. In 645 Pyrrhus, after debating the abbot Maximus the Confessor in North Africa, came to Rome, renounced Monothelitism, and was received by Theodore with honor. When Pyrrhus returned to his former teaching at Ravenna, Theodore excommunicated him in 648. The Byzantine chronicler Theophanes adds that he signed the sentence with ink mixed with consecrated wine, a detail historians cannot confirm.

Theodore also declared Paul II deposed. In response, Emperor Constans II issued the Typos in 648, which withdrew the Ekthesis but forbade anyone to discuss whether Christ had one will or two, under heavy penalties.

sections.h2: Preparing the Lateran Council of 649
paras: Rejecting the Typos' imposed silence, Theodore began planning a council in Rome to set out the teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will. He died on 14 May 649 before it could meet. His successor, Martin I, convened the Lateran Council that October, and its decrees carried Theodore's program forward.

In Rome Theodore completed the Oratory of San Venanzio begun by John IV and is credited with the chapel of Saints Primus and Felician at Santo Stefano Rotondo, where a mosaic from his time survives. He was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Reign: 24 November 642 – 14 May 649
Born in Jerusalem; Greek by origin
Excommunicated Patriarch Pyrrhus (648) and declared Paul II deposed
Opposed the Typos of Constans II (648)
Planned the Lateran Council of 649, held after his death under Martin I

faqs.question: Did Pope Theodore I hold the Lateran Council?
faqs.answer: No. He planned it, but he died in May 649. Pope Martin I convened it in October of that year.

faqs.question: What was the Typos of 648?
faqs.answer: It was a decree of Emperor Constans II that withdrew the earlier Ekthesis but banned all discussion of one or two wills in Christ. Theodore and his successors rejected it for silencing orthodox teaching along with error.

faqs.question: Who was Pyrrhus?
faqs.answer: Pyrrhus was a patriarch of Constantinople who supported Monothelitism. He renounced it in Rome before Theodore I in 645, then returned to it, and Theodore excommunicated him in 648.

directAnswer: Pope St. Martin I reigned from 649 to 655. He convened the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned Monothelitism and the emperor's decree forbidding debate on Christ's two wills; for this he was arrested by imperial agents, tried in Constantinople, and exiled to Crimea, where he died. He is the last pope venerated as a martyr.

sections.h2: From Todi to the Throne of Peter
paras: Martin was born near Todi in Umbria. Before his election he served as papal envoy to Constantinople, which gave him firsthand knowledge of the court and of the Christological disputes there. Elected after Theodore I's death in 649, he was consecrated in July without waiting for confirmation from Emperor Constans II, a step that Constantinople treated as defiance.

sections.h2: The Lateran Council of 649
paras: In October 649 Martin opened a council at the Lateran Basilica attended by about 105 bishops, mostly from Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, and North Africa, along with Greek monks living in Rome; the thought of Maximus the Confessor deeply shaped its work. The council taught that Christ, being fully God and fully man, has two natural wills and two natural operations, divine and human, united without confusion or division.

It condemned Monothelitism and anathematized its leading proponents, including Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul of Constantinople. It also rejected both the Ekthesis of Heraclius and the Typos of Constans II. Martin sent the decrees throughout the West and to the East, and the emperor regarded the council as an open challenge to his authority.

sections.h2: Arrest, Trial, and Exile to Crimea
paras: Constans II first ordered the exarch Olympius to arrest the pope, but Olympius instead came to terms with Martin and later rebelled against the emperor. In June 653 a new exarch, Theodore Calliopas, seized Martin, who was ill, in the Lateran and sent him by sea to Constantinople. After a long journey that included a stay on the island of Naxos, he arrived in the capital and was held in prison for months.

He was tried not for doctrine but for treason, accused of supporting Olympius. Condemned, he was publicly stripped of his insignia and paraded through the city. The dying patriarch Paul II is reported to have asked the emperor to spare his life, and the death sentence was changed to exile. Martin was sent to Cherson in Crimea, where his surviving letters describe hunger, illness, and a sense of abandonment. He died there on 16 September 655.

sections.h2: Veneration as Martyr and Saint
paras: While Martin was still alive in exile, the Roman clergy, under imperial pressure, elected Eugene I in 654; Martin appears to have accepted the arrangement. After his death he was honored in both East and West as a martyr for the faith, and he is the last pope the Church venerates as such. The teaching he defended was vindicated by the Third Council of Constantinople in 680–681. In the General Roman Calendar his memorial is April 13; before the 1969 reform it was kept on November 12. Eastern Churches also commemorate him.

keyFacts: Reign: 21 July 649 – 16 September 655
Born near Todi, Umbria; former papal envoy to Constantinople
Convened the Lateran Council of October 649 against Monothelitism
Arrested in 653, tried in Constantinople, exiled to Cherson in Crimea
Last pope venerated as a martyr; memorial April 13 (formerly November 12)

faqs.question: Why was Pope Martin I arrested?
faqs.answer: He convened the Lateran Council of 649, which condemned the emperor's Typos and the Monothelite teaching it protected. Constans II had him seized in 653, and in Constantinople he was formally charged with treason rather than with any doctrinal error.

faqs.question: Where did Pope St. Martin I die?
faqs.answer: He died in exile at Cherson, an imperial outpost on the Crimean peninsula, in September 655, worn down by hunger and illness.

faqs.question: Why is Martin I considered a martyr?
faqs.answer: He died in exile as a result of persecution for defending the Church's teaching that Christ has a human and a divine will. The Church honors him as a martyr, and he is the most recent pope to receive that title.

directAnswer: Pope St. Eugene I, a Roman cleric, was elected in 654 while his predecessor Martin I was still alive in exile, and he reigned until 657. His legates in Constantinople accepted a compromise statement on the wills of Christ, but the Roman clergy and people rejected it and Eugene did not endorse it.

sections.h2: Elected While Martin I Lived
paras: Eugene was a Roman who had served in the Church from his youth, according to the Liber Pontificalis, which describes him as gentle, kind, and generous. After Martin I was carried off to Constantinople, the Roman clergy delayed for more than a year but, under pressure from the emperor, elected Eugene in August 654. Martin, still alive in exile, seems to have accepted the choice. Eugene's position was delicate: the emperor expected him to be more accommodating than his predecessor.

sections.h2: The Roman Clergy Reject a Compromise
paras: Eugene sent legates to Constantinople to restore relations. They agreed to communion with Patriarch Peter, who offered a formula speaking of two wills and also of one will in Christ, an attempt to bridge the opposing positions. When Peter's synodical letter was read in Santa Maria Maggiore in 656, the clergy and people of Rome rejected it so strongly that they would not let Eugene finish Mass until he promised not to accept it.

Constans II was reportedly angered and threatened to deal with Eugene as he had with Martin, but war with the Arabs occupied him. Eugene died on 2 June 657, which is his feast day, and was buried in St. Peter's. Little more is known about him.

keyFacts: Reign: 10 August 654 – 2 June 657
Born in Rome
Elected while Pope St. Martin I was still alive in exile
Roman clergy and people rejected Patriarch Peter's compromise formula (656)
Feast day June 2

faqs.question: How could Eugene I be elected while Martin I was alive?
faqs.answer: Martin had been removed by force and exiled, and the Roman clergy, under imperial pressure, elected Eugene in 654. Martin appears to have acquiesced, and Eugene is recognized as a legitimate pope.

faqs.question: Did Eugene I accept Monothelitism?
faqs.answer: No. His legates in Constantinople went along with an ambiguous formula, but when it reached Rome the clergy and people rejected it and Eugene promised not to accept it.

directAnswer: Pope St. Vitalian, from Segni, reigned from 657 to 672. He restored working relations with Constantinople, received Emperor Constans II in Rome in 663, and shaped the English church by consecrating Theodore of Tarsus as archbishop of Canterbury in 668.

sections.h2: Restoring Ties with Constantinople
paras: Vitalian was born at Segni in Lazio. Elected in the summer of 657, he received imperial confirmation quickly and sent the customary letters announcing his election to Emperor Constans II and Patriarch Peter, avoiding direct argument over the wills of Christ. In return the emperor sent a gift of a Gospel book, and Vitalian's name was entered in the diptychs, the lists of bishops commemorated in the liturgy at Constantinople, a rare mark of favor for a pope in these years of dispute.

In July 663 Constans II came to Rome, the first emperor to visit the city in nearly two centuries. Vitalian received him with honor, and the emperor attended Mass at St. Peter's. Before leaving after about twelve days, however, he had bronze stripped from Roman monuments, including the roof tiles of the Pantheon, and shipped away.

sections.h2: Ravenna's Bid for Independence
paras: Relations soured over Ravenna, the seat of imperial government in Italy. In 666 Constans II granted its archbishop, Maurus, independence from papal jurisdiction. Vitalian and Maurus exchanged excommunications, and the dispute continued until the decree was withdrawn under Constantine IV some years later. When Constans was murdered in Sicily in 668, Vitalian supported his son Constantine IV against the usurper Mezezius.

sections.h2: Theodore of Tarsus and the English Church
paras: In England, the Synod of Whitby in 664 had led Northumbria to follow Roman practice on the date of Easter. When Wighard, chosen to be archbishop of Canterbury, died in Rome before consecration, Vitalian selected Theodore, a learned Greek monk from Tarsus then living in Rome, and consecrated him in March 668. He sent with him Hadrian, an abbot of African origin. Bede credits the two with organizing the English church and founding a school at Canterbury renowned for Greek and Latin learning.
Vitalian died on 27 January 672, his feast day, and was buried in St. Peter's. Later tradition credits him with introducing the organ into church worship, but there is no early evidence for this.

keyFacts: Reign: 30 July 657 – 27 January 672
Born at Segni, Lazio
Received Emperor Constans II in Rome in 663
Opposed Ravenna's grant of independence from Rome (666)
Consecrated Theodore of Tarsus as archbishop of Canterbury (668); feast day January 27

faqs.question: How did Pope Vitalian influence the Church in England?
faqs.answer: He chose and consecrated Theodore of Tarsus as archbishop of Canterbury in 668 and sent him with the abbot Hadrian. Theodore unified the English dioceses, and their school at Canterbury became a major center of learning.

faqs.question: What happened when Emperor Constans II visited Rome?
faqs.answer: Vitalian welcomed him in 663 and the emperor took part in worship at St. Peter's, but he also removed bronze from Roman buildings, including the Pantheon's roof tiles, and carried it off.

faqs.question: Did Pope Vitalian introduce the organ into churches?
faqs.answer: A later tradition says so, but no early source supports it, and historians treat the claim as unproven.

directAnswer: Pope Adeodatus II was a Roman monk who reigned from 672 to 676. The Liber Pontificalis remembers him for his kindness to clergy and pilgrims and for restoring churches, and he refused to accept letters from Constantinople that reflected Monothelite teaching.

sections.h2: A Monk of St. Erasmus on the Caelian Hill
paras: Adeodatus was the son of a Roman named Jovinian and became a monk at the monastery of St. Erasmus on the Caelian Hill. Because of this, he is sometimes listed as a Benedictine, though the monastery's rule in this period is uncertain. As pope he enlarged St. Erasmus and granted it endowments. He is sometimes called simply Adeodatus, since his predecessor Adeodatus I is also known as Deusdedit.

sections.h2: Generosity and Firmness
paras: The Liber Pontificalis praises his generosity: he increased the customary gift to the clergy and welcomed pilgrims and the poor warmly. He restored the church of St. Peter on the Via Portuensis and dedicated it anew. The same source records that he would not receive the synodical letters of the patriarch of Constantinople, since they still reflected Monothelite views, so relations between Rome and the imperial church remained cool.
He died on 17 June 676 and was buried in St. Peter's. Little else is known about his pontificate.

keyFacts: Reign: 11 April 672 – 17 June 676
Born in Rome, son of Jovinian
Monk of the monastery of St. Erasmus on the Caelian Hill
Restored the church of St. Peter on the Via Portuensis
Refused Monothelite letters from Constantinople

faqs.question: Why is Adeodatus II sometimes called just Adeodatus?
faqs.answer: His predecessor Adeodatus I is often called Deusdedit, so some lists count this pope as the only Adeodatus and omit the numeral.

faqs.question: Was Adeodatus II a Benedictine?
faqs.answer: He was a monk at St. Erasmus in Rome and is often counted as a Benedictine, but which rule that monastery followed in the seventh century is not certain.

directAnswer: Pope Donus was a Roman who reigned from 676 to 678. The Liber Pontificalis records his restoration of Roman churches, including paving the atrium of St. Peter's with marble, and the return of the archbishop of Ravenna to obedience to Rome.

sections.h2: Marble for the Atrium of St. Peter's
paras: Donus was the son of a Roman named Mauricius and was elderly when he was consecrated in November 676, after a vacancy of more than four months. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with paving the great atrium in front of St. Peter's, known as the paradise, with marble, and with restoring other churches, including the church of the Apostles on the Via Ostiensis and Sant'Eufemia on the Via Appia.

sections.h2: Ravenna's Return and Nestorian Monks in Rome
paras: During his reign, the same source says, Archbishop Reparatus of Ravenna returned to obedience to the Roman see, beginning the end of the independence Ravenna had claimed under Pope Vitalian. Donus also discovered that a monastery in Rome known as the Boetiana housed Syrian monks holding Nestorian views; he dispersed them among other monasteries and gave the house to Roman monks.

Emperor Constantine IV wrote to Donus proposing a conference to settle the dispute over Christ's wills, a step that would lead to the Third Council of Constantinople, but the letter arrived only after Donus had died on 11 April 678. He was buried in St. Peter's. Little else is known of him.

keyFacts: Reign: 2 November 676 – 11 April 678
Born in Rome, son of Mauricius
Paved the atrium of Old St. Peter's with marble
Archbishop Reparatus of Ravenna returned to obedience to Rome
Constantine IV's letter proposing a council arrived after his death

faqs.question: What did Pope Donus do for St. Peter's Basilica?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, he paved the large courtyard in front of Old St. Peter's, called the paradise, with marble.

faqs.question: How did Donus' reign affect Ravenna?
faqs.answer: Archbishop Reparatus of Ravenna, whose see had been granted independence from Rome under Constans II, returned to obedience to the pope during Donus' pontificate.

directAnswer: Pope St. Agatho, a Sicilian of Greek background, reigned from 678 to 681. His dogmatic letter on the two wills of Christ was accepted by the Third Council of Constantinople, the sixth ecumenical council, which ended the Monothelite controversy; he also heard St. Wilfrid's appeal and sent a Roman chant master to England.

sections.h2: A Sicilian Monk Elected Pope
paras: Agatho was born in Sicily and, according to some sources, was a monk before his election; the Liber Pontificalis describes him as gentle and kind to all. He took office in June 678, shortly after Emperor Constantine IV had written to Rome proposing a conference to resolve the long dispute over whether Christ had one will or two. Agatho seized the opportunity.

sections.h2: The Letter That Shaped the Sixth Ecumenical Council
paras: Before sending delegates east, Agatho gathered the bishops of the West. A large synod met in Rome around Easter 680, and regional councils in places such as Milan and Hatfield in England sent their professions of faith. Agatho then sent legates to Constantinople with two letters: one in his own name setting out the teaching that Christ has a divine will and a human will, and one from the Roman synod.

The Third Council of Constantinople opened in November 680. Agatho's letter was read and examined, and the bishops accepted it as an expression of the true faith, famously declaring that Peter had spoken through Agatho. The council defined the doctrine of two wills and two operations in Christ and condemned the leaders of Monothelitism. Agatho did not live to see its conclusion; he died on 10 January 681, and the council closed in September of that year.

sections.h2: St. Wilfrid's Appeal and Chant for England
paras: Agatho also intervened in England. Wilfrid, bishop of York, had been removed and his diocese divided by Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury; he traveled to Rome to appeal, and a synod under Agatho in 679 ruled that he should be restored. The decision was not enforced in Northumbria, but it is an early instance of an English bishop appealing to Rome.

Bede records that Agatho sent John, archcantor of St. Peter's and abbot of St. Martin's in Rome, to England with Benedict Biscop. John taught the Roman way of singing the liturgy to the monks of Wearmouth and also reported to Rome on the orthodoxy of the English church. Agatho is venerated as a saint in both East and West; his feast in the Roman Church is January 10.

keyFacts: Reign: 27 June 678 – 10 January 681
Born in Sicily; Greek background
His dogmatic letter was accepted by the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681)
Roman synod of 679 upheld St. Wilfrid's appeal
Feast day January 10; also venerated in the East

faqs.question: What was Pope Agatho's role at the Third Council of Constantinople?
faqs.answer: He did not attend in person, but his legates presented his letter on the two wills of Christ. The council accepted it as the orthodox faith and used it to condemn Monothelitism.

faqs.question: What does 'Peter has spoken through Agatho' mean?
faqs.answer: It was the council fathers' acclamation after hearing Agatho's letter. They recognized in it the faith of the apostle Peter, a phrase often cited as early Eastern recognition of the teaching authority of the bishop of Rome.

faqs.question: Did Agatho live to see the end of the council?
faqs.answer: No. He died in January 681, while the council was still meeting. His successor Leo II confirmed its decrees.

directAnswer: Pope St. Leo II, a Sicilian, reigned from 682 to 683. He confirmed the decrees of the Third Council of Constantinople, had them translated into Latin and accepted in the West, and secured the end of Ravenna's independence from the Roman see.

sections.h2: A Scholar of Greek, Latin, and Chant
paras: Leo was born in Sicily, the son of a man named Paul. The Liber Pontificalis praises him as eloquent, learned in Scripture, fluent in both Greek and Latin, and skilled in chant and psalmody. Although he was elected soon after Pope Agatho died in January 681, he was not consecrated until August 682, largely because confirmation had to wait for the end of the council in Constantinople and the return of the papal legates.

sections.h2: Confirming the Sixth Ecumenical Council
paras: Leo's chief task was to confirm the Third Council of Constantinople. He translated its acts into Latin and wrote to Emperor Constantine IV approving its definition of two wills in Christ. He also wrote to the bishops of Spain and to Visigothic leaders asking them to accept the council, which a Spanish council at Toledo did in 684.

In these letters Leo joined in the council's condemnation of Honorius I, but he framed it carefully: Honorius was blamed for failing to extinguish the heresy and allowing the faith to be compromised, rather than for teaching heresy himself. Theologians have since relied on his wording when discussing Honorius.

sections.h2: Ending Ravenna's Autocephaly
paras: Constantine IV withdrew the earlier decree that had freed the archbishop of Ravenna from papal authority. Under the new arrangement, archbishops of Ravenna were again to be consecrated in Rome, while Leo abolished the fee formerly charged for the pallium and ceremonies connected with it. In Rome he is credited with building a church in honor of St. Paul and moving relics there.
Leo died on 28 June 683 after less than a year in office and was buried in St. Peter's. He is venerated as a saint and has traditionally been commemorated on July 3.

keyFacts: Reign: 17 August 682 – 28 June 683
Born in Sicily; known for learning in Greek, Latin, and chant
Confirmed and translated the acts of the Third Council of Constantinople
Explained Honorius I's condemnation as negligence rather than heresy
Ended Ravenna's independence from Rome

faqs.question: Why was Leo II's consecration delayed for over a year?
faqs.answer: He was elected after Agatho's death in early 681, but consecration waited for imperial confirmation, which came only after the Third Council of Constantinople ended and the papal legates returned to Rome.

faqs.question: What did Leo II say about Pope Honorius?
faqs.answer: He accepted the council's condemnation but explained that Honorius had failed to suppress the heresy as he should have, rather than teaching it. His phrasing has shaped Catholic discussion of the Honorius case ever since.

directAnswer: Pope St. Benedict II, a Roman priest, reigned from 684 to 685. After waiting about a year for imperial confirmation, he obtained from Emperor Constantine IV a concession that shortened such delays, and he worked to have the Spanish church accept the Third Council of Constantinople.

sections.h2: A Year's Wait and an Imperial Concession
paras: Benedict was a Roman, trained from boyhood in the Church's service and known, according to the Liber Pontificalis, for his knowledge of Scripture and chant, his humility, and his care for the poor. He was elected soon after Leo II's death in June 683 but could not be consecrated until June 684, when the emperor's approval finally arrived.

That long wait seems to have prompted a change. Emperor Constantine IV issued a decree allowing a newly elected pope to be consecrated without waiting for confirmation from Constantinople, with approval left to the exarch in Ravenna or dispensed with altogether; historians differ on the exact terms. The Liber Pontificalis adds that the emperor sent locks of hair from his sons Justinian and Heraclius, a gesture placing them under the pope's spiritual patronage.

sections.h2: Spain and the Sixth Ecumenical Council
paras: Benedict continued Leo II's effort to win Spanish acceptance of the Third Council of Constantinople. Archbishop Julian of Toledo sent a statement of faith that Benedict found unclear in places, and Julian later defended it at a council in Toledo after Benedict's death. The pope also restored several Roman churches.
Benedict died on 8 May 685 and was buried in St. Peter's. He is venerated as a saint, with his feast kept on May 7. Little more is known of his eleven-month reign.

keyFacts: Reign: 26 June 684 – 8 May 685
Born in Rome
Waited about a year for imperial confirmation after his election
Obtained a decree from Constantine IV easing the confirmation of papal elections
Feast day May 7

faqs.question: What changed in papal elections under Benedict II?
faqs.answer: Emperor Constantine IV issued a decree that allowed a pope-elect to be consecrated without waiting for approval from Constantinople. Its precise terms are debated, but it shortened the long vacancies of the seventh century.

faqs.question: Why did Constantine IV send his sons' hair to Benedict II?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, the locks of hair symbolized placing the emperor's sons Justinian and Heraclius under the pope's spiritual care, a customary sign of honor and adoption.

directAnswer: Pope John V, a Syrian from the region of Antioch, reigned from 685 to 686. A former papal legate to the Third Council of Constantinople, he was the first pope consecrated without the long wait for imperial confirmation, but illness kept him confined for most of his year in office.

sections.h2: Legate to the Sixth Ecumenical Council
paras: John was born in Syria, in the province of Antioch, one of several Eastern clergy who rose in the Roman Church during this period. As a deacon he served as one of Pope Agatho's legates at the Third Council of Constantinople in 680–681 and brought its acts back to Rome. He was elected by the clergy, army, and people gathered at the Lateran in July 685 and consecrated promptly, thanks to the arrangement Benedict II had obtained from the emperor.

sections.h2: Tax Relief and the See of Cagliari
paras: The Liber Pontificalis describes John as learned and moderate. During his reign the emperor reduced the taxes owed on the papal estates in Sicily and Calabria, and John distributed generous gifts to the clergy and to charitable institutions. He also asserted Roman authority over the church of Sardinia after the archbishop of Cagliari consecrated a bishop without papal approval.
Most of his pontificate, however, was spent in sickness. He died on 2 August 686 and was buried in St. Peter's. Beyond these points, little is known.

keyFacts: Reign: 23 July 685 – 2 August 686
Born in Syria, in the region of Antioch
Served as papal legate at the Third Council of Constantinople
First pope consecrated under the new, faster confirmation procedure
Ill for most of his pontificate

faqs.question: What role did John V play before becoming pope?
faqs.answer: As a deacon he was one of Pope Agatho's legates at the Third Council of Constantinople, which condemned Monothelitism, and he carried the council's acts back to Rome.

faqs.question: Why is John V counted among the Eastern popes?
faqs.answer: He was a Syrian from the Antioch region, part of a series of popes of Greek or Syrian background who led the Church between the mid-seventh and mid-eighth centuries.

directAnswer: Pope Conon reigned from 686 to 687. The son of a Thracian officer, educated in Sicily, he was chosen as a compromise between rival candidates of the Roman clergy and army, and he was elderly and ill throughout his brief pontificate.

sections.h2: A Compromise Between Clergy and Army
paras: Conon's father was an officer from the Thracesian theme, and Conon was educated in Sicily before being ordained in Rome. After John V's death, the clergy supported the archpriest Peter while the army backed a priest named Theodore, and the two sides could not agree. The Liber Pontificalis says the clergy finally turned to Conon, an old man respected for his venerable appearance and simple life, and the army accepted him.

sections.h2: A Short and Troubled Reign
paras: Emperor Justinian II showed him favor, reducing taxes on papal lands in southern Italy and releasing tenants held as security for unpaid dues. Conon, however, angered the Roman clergy by appointing a deacon of Syracuse named Constantine as administrator of the Church's Sicilian estates, an appointment that led to disorder there.

Tradition holds that the Irish missionary St. Kilian came to Rome during this pontificate and received a commission from Conon to preach in Franconia. Conon was sick for most of his reign and died on 21 September 687. His death set off a disputed election that ended with the choice of Sergius I. Little else is known.

keyFacts: Reign: 21 October 686 – 21 September 687
Son of a Thracian officer; educated in Sicily
Elected as a compromise between clergy and army candidates
Justinian II reduced taxes on papal estates during his reign
Tradition links him to the mission of St. Kilian to Franconia

faqs.question: Why was Pope Conon chosen?
faqs.answer: The Roman clergy and army backed different candidates and reached a deadlock. Conon, an elderly and widely respected priest, was put forward as a compromise and accepted by both.

faqs.question: Did Pope Conon send St. Kilian to Germany?
faqs.answer: Tradition says Kilian visited Rome under Conon and was commissioned to evangelize Franconia. The account comes from later lives of Kilian, so the details are not certain.

directAnswer: Pope St. Sergius I, born in Sicily to a Syrian family from Antioch, reigned from 687 to 701. He rejected the canons of the Quinisext Council of 692, survived an imperial attempt to arrest him, added the Agnus Dei to the Roman Mass, and baptized King Caedwalla of Wessex and consecrated St. Willibrord.

sections.h2: Elected Amid Rival Claimants
paras: Sergius was born in Palermo to a family that had come from Antioch in Syria. He came to Rome under Pope Adeodatus II, was trained in the papal chant school, and became priest of the church of Santa Susanna. When Conon died in 687, the archpriest Theodore and the archdeacon Paschal each claimed the papacy with the backing of rival factions. Most of the clergy and people rejected both and elected Sergius, and Theodore soon submitted.

Paschal had secretly promised gold to the exarch John Platyn in exchange for support. The exarch came to Rome, recognized Sergius, and nonetheless demanded the promised sum from the Church before confirming him. Paschal was later deposed from his office for conspiring against the new pope.

sections.h2: Refusing the Canons of the Quinisext Council
paras: In 692 Emperor Justinian II convened a council in the domed hall of the imperial palace in Constantinople, known as the Council in Trullo or Quinisext Council, to issue disciplinary canons. Several canons contradicted Roman practice, among them rules on clerical marriage and on fasting, and one repeated the claim that Constantinople held privileges equal to Rome. Sergius refused to sign the canons or allow them to be read.

The emperor first had two papal advisers seized, then sent an official named Zacharias to bring the pope to Constantinople. Soldiers from Ravenna and the surrounding region rushed to Rome to defend Sergius, and the Liber Pontificalis relates that Zacharias, fearing the crowd, took refuge in the pope's own chamber until Sergius calmed the troops. Justinian II was overthrown in 695, and the matter lapsed.

sections.h2: The Agnus Dei and the Marian Feasts
paras: Sergius left a lasting mark on the liturgy. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he ordered that the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, be sung by clergy and people at the breaking of the bread during Mass, a practice familiar in Eastern churches. He also introduced processions in Rome on four feasts of the Virgin Mary: the Annunciation, the Dormition (later the Assumption), her Nativity, and the Presentation of the Lord, also called the Purification.

He restored and decorated many Roman churches, and the same source says he found a relic of the True Cross in a neglected reliquary in St. Peter's. During his reign the Synod of Pavia, held around 698, brought the bishops of the province of Aquileia back into communion, ending the long schism over the Three Chapters.

sections.h2: Caedwalla and Willibrord
paras: Sergius had close ties with the English. In 689 King Caedwalla of Wessex abdicated, traveled to Rome, and was baptized by Sergius on Holy Saturday; he died days later and was buried in St. Peter's. In 695 the pope consecrated the Northumbrian monk Willibrord as archbishop of the Frisians, giving him the name Clement and launching an important mission in the Low Countries. Sergius died on 8 September 701 and is venerated as a saint on that date.

keyFacts: Reign: 15 December 687 – 8 September 701
Born in Palermo to a Syrian family from Antioch
Refused the canons of the Quinisext Council (692)
Introduced the singing of the Agnus Dei at Mass
Baptized King Caedwalla of Wessex (689) and consecrated St. Willibrord (695)

faqs.question: Did Pope Sergius I add the Lamb of God to the Mass?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Liber Pontificalis says Sergius ordered the Agnus Dei to be sung at the breaking of the bread, and the prayer has remained part of the Roman Mass ever since.

faqs.question: Why did Justinian II try to arrest Sergius I?
faqs.answer: Sergius refused to approve the canons of the Quinisext Council of 692, several of which conflicted with Roman discipline. The emperor's envoy was blocked by soldiers and citizens who came to the pope's defense.

faqs.question: What was Sergius I's connection to St. Willibrord?
faqs.answer: In 695 Sergius consecrated Willibrord, an English missionary, as archbishop of the Frisians and gave him the name Clement. Willibrord went on to found the see of Utrecht.

directAnswer: Pope John VI, a Greek, reigned from 701 to 705. The Liber Pontificalis records that he protected the exarch of Ravenna from hostile Italian troops, ransomed captives taken by the Lombard duke of Benevento, and upheld the appeal of St. Wilfrid of York.

sections.h2: Shielding the Exarch and Ransoming Captives
paras: John was of Greek origin; later lists say he came from the Greek East, possibly Asia Minor, though details of his early life are not recorded. Soon after his election, the exarch Theophylact arrived in Rome from Sicily, and militia troops from across imperial Italy gathered in a threatening mood. John shut the city gates, sent priests to calm the soldiers, and protected the exarch from harm, according to the Liber Pontificalis.

When Gisulf, the Lombard duke of Benevento, raided Campania, burning and taking captives, John sent clergy with gifts to ransom the prisoners and persuaded the duke to withdraw. The episode shows the pope acting as the main defender of the Roman region in the absence of effective imperial help.

sections.h2: The Final Appeal of Wilfrid of York
paras: In 704 the aged Wilfrid, still in conflict with English church authorities, appealed once more to Rome. A synod under John examined his case at length and found in his favor, and the pope wrote to the kings of Mercia and Northumbria urging that the matter be settled. John died on 11 January 705 and was buried in St. Peter's. Little else is known about him.

keyFacts: Reign: 30 October 701 – 11 January 705
Of Greek origin
Protected the exarch Theophylact from mutinous Italian militia
Ransomed captives from Duke Gisulf of Benevento
Upheld St. Wilfrid's appeal at a Roman synod in 704

faqs.question: How did John VI defend Rome?
faqs.answer: He calmed militia troops threatening the exarch and paid ransom to the Lombard duke Gisulf of Benevento to free captives and persuade him to withdraw from Roman territory.

faqs.question: What was the outcome of Wilfrid's appeal to John VI?
faqs.answer: A Roman synod under John VI ruled in Wilfrid's favor, and the pope wrote to English kings asking them to resolve his case. Wilfrid was eventually reconciled and spent his last years in his monasteries.

directAnswer: Pope John VII, a Greek and the son of a Byzantine official in Rome, reigned from 705 to 707. He is remembered as a patron of art, especially for his chapel to the Virgin in Old St. Peter's and the frescoes of Santa Maria Antiqua, and for returning Justinian II's Quinisext canons without comment.

sections.h2: The Son of the Palatine's Curator
paras: John was the son of Plato, the official responsible for the imperial palace on the Palatine Hill, and he is the first pope known to have been the son of a Byzantine civil official. He had family ties to the old imperial heart of Rome, and as pope he built an episcopal residence on the Palatine above the church of Santa Maria Antiqua. He was the second pope to take the same name as his immediate predecessor.

sections.h2: Patron of Santa Maria Antiqua and the Oratory of the Virgin
paras: John is best known for his artistic commissions. He built an oratory dedicated to the Mother of God inside Old St. Peter's, decorated with mosaics; fragments survive in the Vatican Grottoes and elsewhere, including a portrait of John holding a model of the chapel. He also had Santa Maria Antiqua, in the Roman Forum, richly painted with frescoes, many of which can still be seen today.

When Justinian II returned to power in 705, he sent the canons of the Quinisext Council to Rome, asking the pope to confirm those he could and reject the rest. The Liber Pontificalis says John, out of human weakness, returned them without changes. He died on 18 October 707 and was buried in his chapel at St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Reign: 1 March 705 – 18 October 707
Of Greek origin; son of Plato, curator of the imperial palace on the Palatine
Built an oratory to the Virgin in Old St. Peter's
Commissioned frescoes at Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum
Returned the Quinisext canons to Justinian II without comment

faqs.question: What art survives from Pope John VII?
faqs.answer: Frescoes he commissioned at Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum survive, as do mosaic fragments from his oratory of the Virgin in Old St. Peter's, including a portrait of the pope.

faqs.question: How did John VII respond to the Quinisext canons?
faqs.answer: Justinian II asked him to approve the acceptable canons and reject the rest. According to the Liber Pontificalis, John simply sent them back without any changes.

directAnswer: Pope Sisinnius, a Syrian, reigned for only about three weeks in January and February 708. The Liber Pontificalis says he was so crippled by gout that he could not feed himself, yet he still ordered preparations to repair the walls of Rome.

sections.h2: Twenty Days as Bishop of Rome
paras: Sisinnius was Syrian by birth, and the Liber Pontificalis names his father as John. He was consecrated on 15 January 708 after a vacancy of about three months and died suddenly on 4 February, making his pontificate one of the shortest in Church history.

sections.h2: Gout and the Walls of Rome
paras: The Liber Pontificalis describes him as so afflicted by gout that he could not use his hands to eat, yet it says he was firm of mind and concerned for the city. He ordered lime to be prepared for repairing Rome's walls, a project later taken up by his successors, and he consecrated a bishop for Corsica.
He was buried in St. Peter's. Apart from these few details, nothing else is reliably known about him.

keyFacts: Reign: 15 January 708 – 4 February 708
Syrian by birth
One of the shortest pontificates in history, about twenty days
Severely afflicted by gout, according to the Liber Pontificalis
Ordered preparations to repair the walls of Rome

faqs.question: How long was Pope Sisinnius pope?
faqs.answer: About twenty days, from his consecration on 15 January 708 until his sudden death on 4 February 708.

faqs.question: What did Pope Sisinnius accomplish?
faqs.answer: Despite severe gout, he ordered lime prepared to restore the walls of Rome and consecrated a bishop for Corsica, according to the Liber Pontificalis.

directAnswer: Pope Constantine, a Syrian, reigned from 708 to 715. He traveled to the East at Emperor Justinian II's request in 710–711, reaching a settlement over the Quinisext canons, and he later refused to recognize the Monothelite emperor Philippicus. He was the last pope to visit Constantinople until Paul VI in 1967.

sections.h2: The Journey to Justinian II
paras: Constantine was Syrian by birth, like his short-lived predecessor Sisinnius. In 710 Justinian II summoned him east to resolve the dispute over the canons of the Quinisext Council. The pope set out in October with a group of clergy that included the deacon Gregory, later Pope Gregory II, sailing by way of Naples and Sicily and spending the winter at Otranto.

Constantine was received with great honor in Constantinople, and he met the emperor at Nicomedia, where, the Liber Pontificalis relates, Justinian prostrated himself and kissed the pope's feet. A compromise was reached, with Gregory answering the emperor's questions about the canons, and Justinian renewed the privileges of the Roman Church. Constantine returned to Rome in October 711.

sections.h2: Resisting the Monothelite Emperor Philippicus
paras: Shortly after the pope's return, Justinian II was overthrown and killed. The new emperor, Philippicus Bardanes, revived Monothelitism and rejected the Third Council of Constantinople. Rome refused to accept him: his portrait and name were not admitted in the city's churches or on its documents, and fighting broke out between his supporters and opponents in Rome. When Anastasius II took power in 713, he sent Constantine a statement of orthodox faith, ending the crisis.

sections.h2: Ravenna and Two English Kings
paras: Archbishop Felix of Ravenna had refused the usual pledges of obedience to Rome; after Justinian II's harsh punishment of Ravenna, Felix eventually submitted. Bede records that two English kings, Cenred of Mercia and Offa of the East Saxons, came to Rome during Constantine's reign and became monks there. Constantine died on 9 April 715 and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Reign: 25 March 708 – 9 April 715
Syrian by birth
Traveled to Constantinople and Nicomedia in 710–711 to meet Justinian II
Refused to recognize the Monothelite emperor Philippicus
Last pope to visit Constantinople until Paul VI in 1967

faqs.question: Why did Pope Constantine travel to Constantinople?
faqs.answer: Emperor Justinian II summoned him to settle the dispute over the canons of the Quinisext Council. The visit ended in a compromise and a renewal of the Roman Church's privileges.

faqs.question: Which pope next visited Constantinople after Constantine?
faqs.answer: No pope visited the city again until Paul VI went to Istanbul in 1967, more than twelve and a half centuries later.

faqs.question: Why did Rome reject Emperor Philippicus?
